title: The name at death
hookLine: when there's only strength for one word, Pure Land Buddhists say a name
tomorrow: why do some families count forty-nine days after a death?

cards: When people are badly frightened, a stubbed toe, a skid on ice, a phone call at night, they often say a single word, and it's frequently a name. Mom. A partner's name.
God. A name is what's left when the long sentences are gone. Long sentences need breath.
A name barely does. So what if all you can manage at the end is one name? A large family of Buddhists, the Pure Land schools, build a whole practice on that.

teach.b: The name is Amida, or Amitabha, the Buddha of boundless light.

teach.h: A VOW THAT HOLDS THE NAME.
teach.b: A Pure Land sutra tells of his vows, made long ago: anyone who hears his name and turns to him with sincere trust will be born in his Pure Land, a place where awakening comes easily. Another sutra goes further.
Even someone who has done great wrong, if at death a good friend sits with them and helps them say the name, ten times, will be welcomed there. In Japanese the words are Namu Amida Butsu.
In Vietnamese, Nam mô A Di Đà Phật. That second one is said in Vietnamese homes when someone dies, when someone is sick, sometimes just on hearing hard news.
And families gather at the bedside to say it with the dying, so the last sound they hear is the name.

teach.h: TWO WAYS TO WEIGH THE DEATHBED.
teach.b: Inside Pure Land Buddhism, teachers weigh the deathbed differently.

Some urge saying the name all through life and especially at the end. Shinran, a Japanese teacher, taught that birth in the Pure Land is settled the moment trust arises, so the deathbed isn't what decides.
Either way, the name works like a handrail in the dark: you don't need to see the whole staircase to hold on. It's a door kept open by someone else's vow, not by the strength of the one who's dying.
And anyone at the bedside can say it with them.

how: Pure Land Buddhists in Japan, China, Vietnam and elsewhere recite Amida's name (the nembutsu) daily; at a deathbed, family and temple members often chant it together with the dying person and keep chanting after death.

games.q: what does “the name at death” mean?
o: a secret name each person receives at birth
the name carved on a gravestone after a funeral
saying Amida Buddha's name with someone as they die

games.q: the name at the end — tap the pairs.
p: Nam mô A Di Đà Phật
birth is settled when trust arises

s: in Pure Land teaching, the dying person's own strength is what saves them
the name is a door kept open by Amida's vow, not by the strength of the dying.
a sutra says a good friend at the deathbed can help someone say the name
even someone who has done great wrong, helped by a good friend to say it ten times.
all Pure Land teachers agree the deathbed is what decides
Shinran taught that birth is settled when trust arises, so the deathbed isn't what decides.

games.q: your friend's grandmother, a Pure Land Buddhist, is dying and can barely speak. the family is nervous to say anything. what fits today's teaching?
o: explain the sutra's vows to her in detail, so she understands.
sit with her and softly say the name with her, or for her.
stay quiet; saying the name only counts if she can say it herself.
games.why: the sutra pictures a good friend at the bedside helping with the name. the vow holds it, not her strength, so others can say it with her.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is sick, or someone who has died. If this is your practice, say the name softly for them, Namu Amida Butsu, or Nam mô A Di Đà Phật, on each out-breath.
If it isn't, say that person's own name on each out-breath, slowly, with a kind wish.

wordCard.voice: The name at death: Pure Land Buddhists say Amida's name with the dying, trusting a vow to hold them when their own strength can't.

orig.note: Pali buddhanussati: recollection of the Buddha; nembutsu is the Japanese for this idea.

carryVoice: Pocket line: the name at the end, short enough to say when nothing else is. Day twenty-five, named.

sources.ref: Larger Sukhavativyuha Sutra (Amida's vows; those who hear the name with sincere trust are born in the Pure Land)
Contemplation Sutra (Amitayurdhyana Sutra), the lowest grade of birth: a wrongdoer, helped at death by a good friend, says the name ten times
Shinran's teaching that birth is settled when shinjin (true entrusting) arises, without relying on the deathbed
